summary:
Armenia carries no criminal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct; the provision was repealed in 2003, and the country has no statute of the restrictive type applied in neighbouring Azerbaijan. A 2013 police proposal to criminalise "non-traditional sexual relationships" and LGBT "propaganda" directed at young people, modelled on legislation in another country, failed to pass after a national LGBT organisation argued it functioned as a distraction tactic. Same-sex marriage is prohibited.

The legal framework offers trans visitors little affirmative protection. There is no discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the anti-discrimination bill tabled in 2018 did not pass. Hate-crime protection covering bias-motivated violence is characterised as ambiguous since 2022.

Legal gender recognition exists as an administrative practice and is medicalised. Equaldex records that a legal gender change has been available since 2006 but requires surgery, that gender-affirming care is restricted, and that no non-binary recognition is available.

Enforcement of protective law is weak where it exists at all. Police took roughly twelve hours to respond to a Molotov-cocktail arson attack on a gay-friendly bar in Yerevan in 2012, though two suspects were later detained through CCTV; in November 2018 a Christian LGBT group cancelled planned forums after what it described as constant threats, organised intimidation from political and religious leaders, and insufficient police readiness to protect participants.

Political hostility toward trans people has been explicit and public. Lilit Martirosyan, Armenia's first registered trans woman, addressed the National Assembly on LGBTI discrimination in April 2019 and received death threats by Facebook and email, including calls from members of parliament that she be burned alive; in February 2020 a member of a nationalist party burned incense over the same lectern, denouncing her speech as a desecration.

The Pink Human Rights Defender NGO's annual report for 2024 documents discrimination, torture and inhuman or degrading treatment including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion targeting LGBT people, violations of private and family life, restrictions on education and work rights, and hate speech. Its material on transgender people includes a chapter on the pressure directed at a transgender individual who participated in a beauty pageant.

Social climate indicators are poor. Equaldex scores public acceptance at 5 of 100. A 2012 study found that 55 per cent of Armenians would end a relationship with a friend or relative who came out and that 70 per cent consider LGBT people strange. In 2014 the Iravunk newspaper published a list of dozens of Armenian LGBT Facebook accounts, describing them as "zombies"; the Court of Appeals ruled that the newspaper had offended no one and ordered the plaintiffs to pay 50,000 dram (about US$120) to it.
tangentialFactors:
Armenia's regional position is comparatively moderate on decriminalisation: Equaldex's three-way comparison places it alongside Georgia as having removed criminal penalties while Azerbaijan retains a restrictive framework. That contrast does not extend to protections, since Armenia scores alongside the region in lacking anti-discrimination coverage.

Restrictions on LGBT expression have come from private and institutional actors as much as from the state. Organisers of the Yerevan International Film Festival cancelled the screening of two LGBT-themed films in 2017 after negative public reaction. The 2014 Iravunk case shows the judiciary siding with a publisher that published a list of LGBT people's social-media accounts, imposing costs on the complainants rather than the newspaper.

The ILGA-Europe and COC fact-finding mission report "Forced Out: LGBT People in Armenia" (February 2009) remains a substantial documentation base for the country's structural conditions, covering visibility and coming out, societal and institutional homophobia, media coverage, HIV/AIDS, discrimination, harassment and violence, community organising, and the legislation affecting LGBT people. It is now dated, and later sources do not report a reversal of the patterns it described.
localsOnly:
Residents live with the social consequences of visibility rather than criminal sanction. The 2012 finding that 55 per cent of Armenians would end a relationship with a friend or relative who came out and 70 per cent find LGBT people strange bears directly on family and workplace exposure for anyone living in the country, and the Pink Human Rights Defender NGO's 2024 report records domestic violence and extortion within LGBT people's own environments alongside institutional violations of private and family life, education and work rights.

The legal gender recognition process is available to residents but is conditioned on surgery and is medicalised, and non-binary identity has no legal route. The practical burden of that requirement falls on people resident in Armenia, who must navigate the administrative and medical process locally.

Community organising carries a documented risk of disruption. In November 2018 a Christian LGBT group abandoned its planned forums after organised intimidation from political and religious leaders, and after concluding that police were not prepared to protect participants. The 2019 National Assembly speech by Lilit Martirosyan, and the February 2020 incident at the same lectern, remain reference points for how trans visibility in public institutions is met.

The Pink Human Rights Defender NGO and other national LGBT organisations are the primary reporting channels for the discrimination, torture and degrading treatment, sexual violence and hate speech catalogued in their annual reports, and were the actors who defeated the 2013 proposal to criminalise non-traditional sexual relationships and so-called propaganda.
outOfScopeNotes:
The characterisation of hate-crime protection as "ambiguous" since 2022 rests on an aggregator's assessment rather than on a sourced court ruling or statute text; no case in the inventory resolves how bias-motivated violence is charged and sentenced in practice, and the point should be treated as unresolved.

No source in the inventory addresses document or marker rules for passports and identity cards held by foreign nationals, entry screening at airports and borders, or whether the surgical requirement for legal gender recognition is applied to non-residents. Any statement about how a trans visitor's own documents will be treated on arrival would be an inference, not a sourced finding.

The Equaldex entries on legal gender recognition, restricted gender-affirming care and non-binary non-recognition are undated beyond the 2006 availability year, and the inventory contains no Armenian ministry or medical-regulation document confirming current practice. Public-opinion figures are from 2012 and are more than a decade old.

The 2024 Pink Human Rights Defender NGO report is cited by scope rather than by individual finding; its beauty-pageant chapter is the only trans-specific item identified in the inventory, and the underlying incidents, dates and outcomes are not enumerated here.
